summaryEn: Taiwan's national shipyard and prime contractor for the island's first domestically built submarine. The order book runs to 2031 and the strategic role is unarguable — but the company has lost money for four straight years, pays no dividend, and burned NT$3.81bn of operating cash in a single quarter.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
CSBC Corporation (台灣國際造船, TWSE: 2208) is **Taiwan's national shipyard**. Founded in **November 1973** and **listed in December 2008**, it builds commercial vessels at Kaohsiung and Keelung — and, far more consequentially, it is the **prime contractor for Taiwan's indigenous defence submarine programme**, whose first boat, the **Hai Kun**, is targeted for delivery in the second half of 2026. Its two largest shareholders are arms of the state: the Executive Yuan's **National Development Fund (14.57%)** and the **Ministry of Economic Affairs (11.26%)**.

The strategic importance is not in dispute, and the revenue mix reflects it: **naval and official vessels are roughly 69.7% of revenue, commercial ships about 23.5%**. Visibility is unusually long — at the June 2026 shareholder meeting the company disclosed **16 commercial and 16 military/official vessels on order with delivery schedules extending to 2031** (Kaohsiung to September 2031, Keelung to October 2031), against a backlog of roughly **NT$130bn** and FY2025 revenue of **NT$21.78bn**. Chairman Chen Cheng-hung has said he expects the Hai Kun to be delivered in the second half of 2026 and is confident of returning to profit later that year.

The financial record is the other half of the story, and it is severe. CSBC lost money for **five consecutive years from 2016, totalling NT$13.6bn** — and then lost money again in each of the four years since: annual EPS of **−NT$3.77 (FY2022), −4.32, −2.21 and −NT$1.76 (FY2025)**. It has **paid no dividend since 2015**, and the board resolved **not to pay one for FY2025** either. Trailing return on equity is **−18.6%**. The 2026Q1 result showing a small net profit of **NT$86m (EPS NT$0.07)** came **despite an operating margin of −3.8%** — the profit was non-operating, not operational.

Most importantly, the balance sheet is tight. **2026Q1 operating cash flow was −NT$3.81bn against just NT$1.60bn of cash**, with a **debt ratio of 85.2%** and equity of only **NT$7.29bn** supporting **NT$49.16bn of assets**. Shipbuilding cash flow swings violently with milestone payments, but that is a narrow margin. The honest read: **a strategically indispensable yard with a decade of visible work and a landmark defence programme — carried by state shareholders through nine loss-making years out of ten, priced at 3.3x book while still burning cash.**

CSBC was created in **1973** as part of Taiwan's industrial build-out, when the government decided the island needed the capacity to build large ships itself. Shipbuilding was then a strategic industry in the most literal sense: it required steel, heavy engineering, precision welding and enormous fixed capital, and it gave a country the ability to build its own merchant fleet — and, in time, its own warships. The yards at **Kaohsiung and Keelung** were the physical expression of that policy.

The commercial logic was harder than the strategic one. Global shipbuilding consolidated around **Korean, Japanese and later Chinese yards** operating at a scale CSBC could not match, competing on price for standardised vessels. Orders are won years before delivery, and **steel plate prices move in between** — meaning a contract signed profitably can become a loss to be provisioned before the hull is finished. CSBC's own disclosures describe exactly this: commercial ships have long order-to-delivery cycles and frequently require loss provisions as steel and shipbuilding prices fluctuate, making them the more volatile part of the business. It **listed in 2008**, and from **2016 lost money for five consecutive years, NT$13.6bn in total**.

What changed the company's meaning was not commercial shipbuilding but **defence**. Taiwan's decision to build submarines domestically — after decades of being unable to buy them abroad — made CSBC the **prime contractor for the indigenous defence submarine programme**, and the yard where the first boat, the **Hai Kun**, was built. Alongside it came naval surface vessels, official ships and, more recently, **unmanned surface vessels**, which the company has noted can be built without occupying a dry dock.

That is the transformation: from a struggling merchant yard into **the platform on which Taiwan's naval self-sufficiency depends** — with naval and official work now roughly 70% of revenue, and an order book stretching to 2031. The financial record has not yet caught up with the strategic one.

- **1973 (7 Nov)** — CSBC established as Taiwan's national shipbuilder, with yards at **Kaohsiung and Keelung**.
- **1970s–2000s** — Builds commercial vessels in a global market increasingly dominated by Korean, Japanese and Chinese yards operating at greater scale.
- **2008 (22 Dec)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2208)**.
- **2016–2020** — **Five consecutive loss-making years, totalling NT$13.6bn.** The **National Development Fund injects capital** via a 450-million-share increase, lifting its stake from about 8% to nearly 15% and making it the largest shareholder.
- **2015** — **Last dividend paid (NT$0.5).** None since.
- **2022–2024** — Losses continue: EPS **−NT$3.77 (FY2022), −4.32 (FY2023), −2.21 (FY2024)**.
- **2025** — Losses narrow to **−NT$1.76** for the year; the final two quarters turn marginally positive (**+NT$0.05, +NT$0.17**) as gross margin recovers from **−41.1% to +12.0%**. Board resolves **no dividend**.
- **2026Q1** — Net profit of **NT$86m (EPS NT$0.07)** despite an **operating margin of −3.8%**; **operating cash flow −NT$3.81bn**. Chairman attributes weakness partly to large FX swings.
- **2026 (25 June)** — Shareholder meeting discloses **16 commercial and 16 military/official vessels on order**, with deliveries scheduled to **2031**. Hai Kun submarine targeted for delivery in **H2 2026**.

CSBC's accounts are the clearest example in this collection of **strategic value and financial performance pointing in opposite directions**.

- **Nine loss-making years out of ten.** Five consecutive losses from 2016 totalling **NT$13.6bn**, then four more: annual EPS of **−NT$3.77 (FY2022), −4.32 (FY2023), −2.21 (FY2024), −NT$1.76 (FY2025)**. Trailing return on equity is **−18.6%**.
- **The recovery is real but shallow.** Gross margin improved from **−41.1% (2024Q4) to +12.0% (2025Q4)**, and the last two quarters of FY2025 were marginally profitable. But **2026Q1 slipped back to a 0.1% gross margin and a −3.8% operating margin** — and the **NT$86m net profit that quarter came from non-operating items**, not from operations. Reading the headline EPS of **+NT$0.07** as a turnaround would be a mistake.
- **The most serious number: cash flow.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow was −NT$3.81bn**, against **cash of NT$1.60bn**. Shipbuilding working capital swings hard with milestone payments and this is one quarter, not a trend — but with **equity of only NT$7.29bn** supporting **NT$49.16bn of assets** and a **debt ratio of 85.2%**, the buffer is thin.
- **State shareholders are the backstop.** The **National Development Fund (14.57%)** and **Ministry of Economic Affairs (11.26%)** are the two largest holders, and the Fund's stake reached that level precisely by **injecting capital during the loss years**. This is the practical reason the company continues: the state requires the capability.
- **No dividend since 2015.** The last payment was **NT$0.5 for FY2015**; the board resolved **none for FY2025**. Dividend yield is zero — accurately so.
- **Valuation.** At **NT$18.85 the shares trade at 3.27× book** on negative earnings. The reported P/E has been removed from this page: at **0.00×** on a loss-making trailing period it carries no information.

The financing reality: **a company kept solvent and capitalised because the state needs it to exist** — now with a decade of visible work, but not yet with a business that funds itself.

**Stance: an indispensable national capability with a decade of order visibility and a landmark submarine programme — attached to a company that has lost money in nine of the last ten years and is priced at 3.3x book while still burning cash.**

The bull case:

1. **Strategic monopoly.** CSBC is **the** yard for Taiwan's naval self-sufficiency: prime contractor for the indigenous submarine programme, builder of the **Hai Kun**, and the platform for surface combatants, official vessels and unmanned surface craft. **Naval and official work is ~69.7% of revenue** — this is a defence contractor that happens to have a merchant division.
2. **Visibility almost no manufacturer has.** **16 commercial and 16 military/official vessels on order with deliveries scheduled to 2031**, and a backlog of roughly **NT$130bn** against FY2025 revenue of **NT$21.78bn** — around six years of work.
3. **A credible inflection.** Gross margin recovered from **−41.1% to +12.0%** over 2025, and the chairman has stated he is confident of returning to profit later in 2026, with the Hai Kun delivery targeted for the second half.

The counter-arguments:

- **The loss record is not a blip.** **Five years of losses to 2020 (NT$13.6bn), then four more.** A company that cannot make money with 70% of revenue from cost-plus-adjacent state work has a structural problem, not a cyclical one.
- **Cash is the binding constraint.** **−NT$3.81bn of operating cash flow in 2026Q1 against NT$1.60bn of cash**, an **85.2% debt ratio** and **NT$7.29bn of equity**. Further state capital injections are plausible — and dilutive.
- **The 2026Q1 "profit" was non-operating.** Operating margin was **−3.8%**.
- **Valuation embeds the theme, not the earnings.** **3.27× book** for a business with **−18.6% trailing ROE** and **no dividend since 2015**.

A **policy-vehicle** thesis: own it for what the state needs it to build, not for what it currently earns — and size it for the cash-flow risk.

CSBC builds ships to order, in two businesses with very different economics:

- **Naval and official vessels (~69.7% of revenue).** Submarines, surface combatants and government ships, contracted by the state. This work is strategic rather than competitive — CSBC is the domestic option — and it carries the **indigenous defence submarine programme**, where the company is prime contractor. Programme risk is technical and schedule-related rather than commercial: these are first-of-class builds with no prior template.
- **Commercial vessels (~23.5% of revenue).** Merchant ships sold into a global market dominated by Korean, Japanese and Chinese yards with greater scale. CSBC's own disclosure explains why this segment is the volatile one: **orders are booked years before delivery, and steel plate and shipbuilding prices move in between**, so contracts require **loss provisions** when input costs rise after signing.
- **Adjacent work.** Offshore wind support and **unmanned surface vessels** — the latter notable because, as the company has pointed out, they can be built **without occupying a dry dock**, so they add revenue without consuming the scarcest asset.

The economics are **project accounting on multi-year builds**. Revenue is recognised across a contract's life, which is why **monthly revenue is wildly erratic** — recent months have ranged from **+132% to −82% year-on-year** — and why single months carry almost no information. Profitability depends on **estimating build cost years in advance**, and the historical evidence is that CSBC has repeatedly estimated it too low.

The structural strength is a **protected position in naval work with an order book to 2031**. The structural weakness is that **dry dock capacity is fixed, labour and steel costs are not, and a mispriced multi-year contract cannot be repriced** — which is how a yard with full order books loses money for nine years out of ten. Cash flow follows milestone payments rather than progress, which is why a single quarter can consume **NT$3.81bn**.

Shipbuilding is a scale industry that Taiwan participates in for reasons other than scale.

- **The commercial market is not winnable on merit.** Global merchant shipbuilding is concentrated in **Korea, China and Japan**, where yards operate at volumes that spread fixed costs across far more hulls and command better terms on steel. A mid-sized yard competing for standardised vessels takes price-taker economics into a multi-year fixed-price contract — the reason CSBC's commercial division is described in its own filings as the volatile, provision-prone segment.
- **The naval market is a different business entirely.** Warship and submarine construction is **not open to foreign competition** for a country pursuing self-sufficiency, and for Taiwan it is not open to purchase abroad either — which is precisely why the indigenous submarine programme exists. Here CSBC has **no domestic competitor of comparable capability** for large platforms, though smaller yards such as Lung Teh compete for patrol craft and unmanned vessels.
- **What defence demand looks like now.** Taiwan's defence budget has expanded substantially, with large programmes covering unmanned vessels and naval construction. This is the source of CSBC's order book to 2031 — and it is set by government appropriation rather than by market demand, which cuts both ways: it is durable while policy holds, and it disappears if appropriations lapse. The company has itself publicly urged that special defence budget funding not be interrupted.
- **The comparison that matters.** Elsewhere in this collection, **AIDC (漢翔)** occupies the analogous position in aerospace: a state-linked prime contractor whose value is national capability rather than commercial return. CSBC is the naval equivalent, with a weaker financial record.

CSBC's position is **secure where it is protected and weak where it is not**. The industry truth is that **a yard's fortunes are set years before the revenue arrives**, at the moment a fixed-price contract is signed against costs that have not yet happened — and that a national shipyard's real shareholder is the state that needs it.

**Strengths**
- **Prime contractor for Taiwan's indigenous defence submarine programme**; builder of the **Hai Kun**; ~**69.7% of revenue** from naval and official vessels.
- **Order visibility to 2031** — 16 commercial and 16 military/official vessels; backlog around **NT$130bn** versus FY2025 revenue of **NT$21.78bn**.
- **State shareholders** (National Development Fund 14.57%, Ministry of Economic Affairs 11.26%) that have injected capital through the loss years.

**Weaknesses**
- **Loss-making in nine of the last ten years**: NT$13.6bn over 2016–2020, then EPS **−3.77 / −4.32 / −2.21 / −1.76**.
- **−NT$3.81bn operating cash flow in 2026Q1** against **NT$1.60bn of cash**; **85.2% debt ratio**; equity of only **NT$7.29bn**.
- **No dividend since 2015**; trailing ROE **−18.6%**; commercial shipbuilding structurally sub-scale.

**Opportunities**
- **Hai Kun delivery in H2 2026** and follow-on submarine construction.
- **Expanded defence appropriations**, including large unmanned-vessel programmes.
- **Unmanned surface vessels** that do not consume dry dock capacity; offshore wind support work.

**Threats**
- **Appropriation risk** — the order book depends on defence budgets being passed and sustained.
- **Cost overruns on first-of-class builds** with no prior template.
- **Further dilutive capital raising** if cash burn continues; steel price moves against fixed-price contracts.

- **Liquidity (the most immediate risk).** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of −NT$3.81bn against NT$1.60bn of cash**, with an **85.2% debt ratio** and **NT$7.29bn of equity** against **NT$49.16bn of assets**. Shipbuilding cash flow is lumpy by nature, but the buffer is genuinely thin, and the historical remedy has been **state capital injections that dilute existing shareholders** — the National Development Fund's stake rose from about 8% to nearly 15% exactly that way.
- **Chronic unprofitability, not a cycle.** **Nine loss-making years in ten.** The proximate cause is well documented — multi-year fixed-price contracts signed against costs that subsequently rose — but the pattern's persistence suggests a structural inability to price risk, not bad luck.
- **The apparent turnaround is not yet operational.** **2026Q1's NT$86m net profit accompanied a −3.8% operating margin.** The profit came from non-operating items. Gross margin also fell back to **0.1%** after reaching 12.0% in the prior quarter.
- **First-of-class programme risk.** The submarine programme has no prior domestic template; schedule slippage and cost overruns on such builds are the norm internationally, and CSBC bears contractual exposure to delay.
- **Political and appropriation dependence.** Roughly **70% of revenue** comes from the state. The order book to 2031 is only as firm as the budgets funding it, and the company has publicly urged that special defence funding not be interrupted.
- **Valuation.** **3.27× book** on **−18.6% trailing ROE** with **no dividend**. The price reflects the defence theme; the accounts do not yet support it. The reported P/E of 0.00× has been removed from this page as meaningless on a loss-making basis.

CSBC's outlook rests on a single question: **can a yard that has lost money for nine of ten years convert an order book running to 2031 into actual profit and cash?** The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin, not net profit.** The decisive figure. Operating margin ran **−47.8% (2024Q4) → +7.2% (2025Q4) → −3.8% (2026Q1)**. A sustained positive operating margin would be the first genuine evidence of a turnaround; net profit driven by non-operating items would not.
- **Operating cash flow.** After **−NT$3.81bn in one quarter against NT$1.60bn of cash**, this is the survival metric. Watch whether milestone payments on naval contracts restore it — and watch for any announcement of a capital raise.
- **Hai Kun delivery and follow-on orders.** Delivery is targeted for **H2 2026**. Execution on the first boat determines both the programme's credibility and CSBC's claim on the follow-on construction that underpins the order book.
- **Defence appropriations.** With roughly **70% of revenue** from state work, budget passage is the demand driver. The company has itself flagged the risk of funding interruption.

Bottom line: CSBC is **strategically indispensable and financially fragile at the same time**. It is the prime contractor for Taiwan's first domestically built submarine, holds **16 commercial and 16 military/official vessels on order with deliveries to 2031**, and is backed by **state shareholders who have repeatedly recapitalised it**. It has also **lost money in nine of the last ten years**, **paid no dividend since 2015**, posted a **−3.8% operating margin** in its most recent quarter, and **burned NT$3.81bn of operating cash against NT$1.60bn on hand** — while trading at **3.27× book**. Judge it on **operating margin and operating cash flow**, not on the order book or the headline EPS.
